Dog runs sized for Harmony's narrow lots

Pet turf in Harmony runs $10–$18 per square foot installed as of September 2026. Harmony's Residential Owners Association wrote wildlife coexistence into its founding documents back in 2002, and its narrow, alley-loaded lots leave less room for a dog run than a standard suburban yard, so drainage and placement matter more here than the infill choice.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A community that wrote wildlife coexistence into its rules

Harmony's Residential Owners Association is unusual among Florida HOAs for building guidelines about living alongside local wildlife into its founding paperwork back in 2002 rather than treating it as an afterthought. That doesn't change anything about how a dog run gets installed, but it does mean a fenced pet area backing a preserve buffer or a lake edge is worth keeping tidy and odor-controlled, since Harmony residents notice a yard that draws raccoons or attracts flies more than most.

Zeolite or coated sand: choosing infill for a dog yard

Two infill options do most of the odor-control work on Harmony dog turf: zeolite, a natural mineral that binds ammonia as liquid passes through it, and coated silica sand, where a non-toxic coating resists bacteria growth on the sand grains themselves. Both fit the state's natural-material rule for infill, unlike rubber or other synthetic fill, which the rule reserves strictly for the ground under playground equipment. Zeolite tends to suit yards with heavier daily use since it's actively binding odor compounds, while coated sand works well for a single dog and a more typical rinse schedule, though either one needs the same permeable backing and base underneath to do its job.

Say you have a 260 sq ft alley-side run

A 260 sq ft strip along the garage alley, fenced for two dogs, prices between $2,600 and $4,680 at the published $10–$18 range, with most jobs this size landing near $3,120 to $4,160 using the typical $12–$16 band. That figure includes the deeper drainage base a run this size needs and zeolite infill brushed in at roughly a pound and a half per square foot. Because the alley sits behind the garage rather than facing the street, the run is unlikely to be visible from the front, which usually simplifies the Residential Owners Association's design review compared with a front-yard project.

Fitting a run into an alley-loaded lot

Harmony's original streets were platted with rear alleys feeding the garages, which leaves a narrower side or back strip for a dog run than a conventional subdivision lot offers built around front-loaded driveways instead. A run along that alley fence usually measures under 300 square feet, tight enough that drainage at the low end matters more than it would on a wide-open lawn, since there's less soil area to absorb a fast rinse-down after a dog uses it.

What an undersized base does to a dog yard by August

A Harmony dog run built with a base too shallow to drain fast, or without the fully permeable backing a pet system needs, will hold liquid at the surface no matter how good the infill choice was on paper. The result usually isn't visible right away; it shows up as a smell that gets worse through the first full summer rather than a puddle anyone notices on installation day. By the time an owner traces the odor back to the base, the fix generally means pulling turf and adding drainage rather than just swapping infill, which is a larger repair than getting the depth right the first time would have been.

Grading a dog run toward a drain, not just away from the house

A plain lawn only needs its subgrade sloped away from the foundation, but a Harmony dog run gets graded toward a specific low point or drain instead, since rinse water and urine both need somewhere consistent to go rather than just somewhere away from the house. That drain point is also chosen to keep liquid moving away from a patio slab or pool deck edge, since concrete holds odor differently than turf does and a slab that stays damp near a dog area tends to stain over time. The one to two percent grade itself doesn't change, only the direction it's aimed and the reason behind picking that direction.

Skipping the weed barrier, adding the right infill

A pet area skips the optional weed-fabric layer a plain lawn might use, since fabric under a dog run traps urine at the surface instead of letting it filter into the base rock below. Zeolite or coated silica sand handles odor control within the state's material rule, which limits infill on any residential lot, dog runs included, to sand, rock, shell or a non-toxic coated product. Rubber crumb, sometimes marketed for pet areas elsewhere, isn't an option on an open Harmony yard under that same rule.

Grading toward the drain before the rock goes down

On a Harmony dog run, the drain point gets located and the bare soil graded toward it before any base material arrives on site, reversing the usual order of just grading away from the house and figuring out drainage later. That sequence matters because once rock is compacted in place, correcting a drain location means tearing back out material that just went down, which costs more time than getting the grade right at the start. Strip-out and grading for a run typically take a similar amount of time as for a lawn of the same size; the difference is entirely in which direction the shovel work points.

Checking a dog run's edges after a storm

After heavy rain or wind, a Harmony dog run's perimeter is worth checking specifically, more so than a family lawn's, since a dog will find and worsen a loose edge within days where a lawn with no traffic on it might sit undisturbed for weeks. A lifted corner or a seam that's started to gap gets re-anchored quickly rather than left for the next scheduled maintenance visit, since a determined digger can turn a small gap into a much larger one in a single afternoon.

Questions people ask

Will a dog run near Harmony's conservation areas need extra approval?

If the run backs a preserve buffer or the golf course edge rather than another yard, mention that in the design review submission; the association's own review covers placement, and the state's drip-line rule can apply separately if mature oaks sit nearby.

Does Harmony's wildlife-coexistence guidance restrict fencing for a dog run?

We found no published fencing restriction tied specifically to wildlife coexistence, only the general architectural review every fence goes through regardless of purpose. Confirm fence height and material with the association before building the run's enclosure.
